newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Fed lets Treasuries reign for now.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Fed lets Treasuries reign for now.

text.p: Treasuries can outpace Europe on the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to hold fire on interest rates but investors will have to hurry as the same old rate worries will soon return, analysts said on Wednesday.
While the 10-year T-note/Bund gap can narrow in the short-term, markets will be fixed squarely on economic data and the next Fed policy meeting on July 1 and 2.

"The focus in the U.S. now is just immediately on the July FOMC and on the likelihood of a strong payroll figure at the beginning of June," said Kit Juckes, head of bond and currency strategy at NatWest Capital Markets in London.
"No action now has had a curve impact but has left the market with a pretty solid conviction that rates go up anyway," he said.
Treasuries closed solidly higher in New York on Tuesday after the Federal Open Market Committee meeting and in early trade in Europe on Wednesday they outpaced Bunds.
The 10-year T-note/Bund gap had slimmed to 100 basis points by 0719 GMT, compared with 104 basis points at the close of business on Tuesday.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said that spread could pull in to around 90 basis points near term.
"We've now got a breathing space until the July meeting," he said. "I don't think the outperformance is going to be too major as I don't think there's going to be too much poor news for Bunds."
He said gains beyond the 90 level would be determined by each piece of economic data that came out of the U.S.

"It's very unclear at the moment whether the pause in growth in April is more than just a pause. I wouldn't expect markets to react too dramatically until it is confirmed growth is at a sustainable pace," he said.

Edmonds said the short-end of the U.S. curve had most to gain as it had overdone rate rise expectations while the long bond would continue to be trapped in a range from around 6.75 percent to 7.00 percent.
Juckes at NatWest said that in the longer term, data would show the U.S. economy continuing at a pace that would unnerve bond markets.

"It would be amazing if that was the last rate rise," he said. "The U.S. economy is like a car on a downhill slope without the brakes on. Unless you put something in its way it's not going to slow down on its own."
The Fed raised its federal funds target rate to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent on March 25.
Juckes expected the T-note/Bund gap to push out toward the 130 basis point level longer term.
"We will only go out slowly becasue there is a fair amount of demand on the part of international investors," he said.
David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London, forecast the spread to stay around current levels.
"It's got a pretty firm toehold on the three digit territory," he said.
He did however, expect all bond markets to gain from the Fed's cautious strategy.

"The Fed is making quite a clear statement it's not going to get into the successive rate hike mode they were in 1994," he said. "It is moving cautiously and gradually here and is very mindful about the markets' response," he said. -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
